COURSE TITLE: ADVANCED DISTRIBUTED SYSTEMS
COURSE CODE: CS601
ACADEMIC YEAR: 2025-2026

UNIT 1: Distributed Consensus and the Raft Protocol
Leader Election Mechanism, Split-Brain Resolution, Heartbeat Timers, Log Replication, Quorum Calculation, Commit Index State Transitions.
Distributed consensus ensures all non-faulty nodes agree on state transitions despite message loss or network partitions.
In the Raft consensus algorithm, nodes exist in one of three states: Follower, Candidate, or Leader.
Leader election triggers when randomized heartbeat timers expire without receiving AppendEntries RPCs from the current leader.
A candidate wins an election by receiving votes from a strict majority quorum of (N/2 + 1) nodes.
Split-brain scenarios are resolved by requiring term monotonicity; requests bearing outdated terms are rejected immediately.
Log entries are committed only when safely replicated across a quorum of operational nodes.

UNIT 2: Database Storage Engines and Log-Structured Merge Trees
LSM-Tree Write Path, MemTable Operations, Write-Ahead Logging (WAL), Immutable SSTables, Compaction Strategies, Bloom Filter Query Optimization.
Modern distributed storage systems utilize Log-Structured Merge (LSM) trees to optimize write-intensive operational workloads.
Incoming mutations append sequentially to an in-memory MemTable and a concurrent Write-Ahead Log (WAL) for durability.
When the MemTable reaches its capacity threshold, it flushes to persistent disk storage as an immutable Sorted String Table (SSTable).
Read operations inspect Bloom filters to avoid unnecessary disk I/O lookups for non-existent keys.
Compaction processes (Size-Tiered or Leveled Compaction) merge overlapping SSTables in the background to purge tombstoned entries and reclaim disk space.
Compaction induces write amplification, which trade-offs disk write throughput for sustained read latency.

UNIT 3: Microservices Resiliency and Circuit Breaker Architectures
Cascade Failure Dynamics, Circuit Breaker State Transitions (Closed, Open, Half-Open), Failure Rate Thresholds, Fallback Degradation, Distributed Tracing Context.
Microservices architectures prevent cascading failures across downstream dependencies using automated circuit breakers.
A circuit breaker monitors downstream call failures within a rolling time window.
In the Closed state, requests pass through normally while error counters accumulate.
When the failure rate breaches a configured threshold (e.g. 50% errors over 20 calls), the breaker transitions to the Open state.
In the Open state, calls fail fast immediately without dispatching network requests, invoking a fallback method to preserve client responsiveness.
After a reset timeout duration, the breaker enters the Half-Open state, permitting a limited probe trial of canary requests.
If probe calls succeed, the circuit resets to Closed; persistent errors trip it back to Open.
